opus-5.5.text:
Ege Erdil: I think the base model matters a lot more than people sometimes assume when they talk about reasoning. There's been a tendency to frame it as either you scale pretraining or you scale reinforcement learning on reasoning, as if they're substitutes. I see them more as complements.

When you do RL on chains of thought, you're mostly not teaching the model brand new capabilities from scratch. You're eliciting and sharpening behaviors that are already latent in the base model: breaking a problem into steps, checking its own work, backtracking when something looks wrong. A larger base model has a richer repertoire of those behaviors to begin with, and it has more world knowledge to reason *about*. So the same amount of RL compute gets you further on a stronger base.

There's also a sample-efficiency point. A bigger model tends to find the reward signal faster during RL because its initial attempts are more often partially correct, so you get more useful gradient signal per rollout. With a weak base model, a lot of RL compute is spent on attempts that are hopeless.

That said, I don't think it's simply "make the base model bigger and everything follows." The gains from reasoning training on top of the base model have been very large relative to what you'd get from an equivalent increase in pretraining compute, at least on things like math and coding where you can verify answers. So my expectation for something like GPT-5 is that the big jumps come from combining the two: a somewhat larger, better-trained base model, plus a lot more inference-time and RL compute layered on top. Where I'd be more cautious is in extrapolating that to tasks without clean verification signals, like long-horizon agentic work in messy real-world settings. There the base model's general knowledge and judgment probably carry more of the weight, and RL hasn't yet shown the same dramatic returns.

r001.rationale: The response says a larger, stronger base model can improve reasoning and help RL, but describes the expected GPT-5 base model as “somewhat larger,” not much larger.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing to understand is that the reasoning models we've seen so far, the o1 and o3 line and whatever ends up in GPT-5, are built on top of a base model, and the quality of that base model puts a ceiling on how far the reinforcement learning on reasoning can take you.

The RL stage is mostly teaching the model to use capabilities it already has in a more organized way. It learns to check its work, to back up when a line of attack isn't going anywhere, to spend more tokens on hard problems. That's genuinely valuable, and the gains on math and coding benchmarks have been large. But the RL is sampling from the distribution the base model already represents and reinforcing the trajectories that happen to work. If the base model has a poor grasp of some domain, there aren't many good trajectories to reinforce, and you can't bootstrap your way out of that with RL alone, at least not efficiently.

So what a larger base model gives you is a richer prior. It knows more facts, it has better internal representations of the structure of problems, it's less likely to make the kind of basic error that derails a long chain of reasoning. When you then do the RL on top, two things happen. First, the starting point is higher, so the same amount of RL compute gets you further. Second, and I think this is underappreciated, the RL becomes more sample efficient, because a larger fraction of the sampled attempts are actually correct or close to correct, and that's what gives you signal.

There's a rough analogy to what happened with pretraining and then instruction tuning. Instruction tuning on a small model gets you something that follows instructions badly. The same recipe on a much larger model gets you something that follows instructions well, even though the tuning data is similar. The base model is doing most of the work. I'd expect reasoning to look similar: the recipe matters, but the recipe applied to a bigger and better base is where most of the capability comes from.

The complication is cost. If you make the base model, say, ten times larger, then every token of reasoning costs ten times more to generate, and these models are generating a lot of tokens. So there's a real tradeoff between scaling the base and scaling inference-time compute, and the labs are going to be making that tradeoff empirically. My guess is that for the next generation or two, both are going to keep scaling, because the returns to both still seem to be there. But I'd be surprised if the frontier reasoning systems in a couple of years are sitting on base models the same size as today's. The larger base is where a lot of the generality is going to come from, and generality is the thing the current reasoning models are weakest on. They're very good at math competition problems and much less obviously improved at things that don't have a clean verifier.

r001.rationale: The candidate says reasoning models, including whatever becomes GPT-5, are built on a base model, and argues that a larger, better base model would contribute substantial reasoning capability.

astra-6.text:
I think larger base models probably help in two ways. One is that they give you a stronger starting point: the model knows more, has better abstractions, and is more likely to find a useful approach to a difficult problem. The other is that they can make the training you do afterward more effective. If you’re using reinforcement learning to train reasoning, it helps if the base model already has some chance of solving the problems you’re training on. Then you have successful attempts to reinforce.

But I wouldn’t think of reasoning as something that comes just from making the base model bigger. There’s also how you train it to use a sequence of intermediate steps, and how much computation you let it spend on a particular question. Those things interact. A stronger base model might get more out of the same amount of thinking, or solve problems that a weaker model can’t solve even if you give it a lot more time.

So, for something like GPT-5, I’d expect improvements to the base model to contribute, potentially quite substantially. But I wouldn’t claim to know how much of the improvement would come from that versus better reasoning training or more computation at inference time.

r001.rationale: The response says a stronger, larger base model can contribute substantially to GPT-5’s reasoning improvements by providing a stronger starting point and helping reasoning training succeed.

sol-6.1.text:
I think larger base models help in two ways. One is that they give you a better starting point: the model knows more, makes fewer basic mistakes, and can recognize more of the patterns that are useful for solving a problem. The other is that they can make additional computation at inference time more productive. If you train a model to work through a problem, check its answer, and try a different approach when it gets stuck, you still need the underlying model to be capable of taking useful steps.

So I wouldn’t think of scaling the base model and training it to reason as separate alternatives. They’re complementary. A stronger base model can potentially learn better reasoning strategies, and those strategies can let you get more out of the capabilities it already has.

For GPT-5 specifically, I’d be cautious about attributing improvements to one ingredient without knowing the training details. You’d want to distinguish improvements from a larger base model, better training after pretraining, and simply spending more computation on each question. All three could matter.

r001.rationale: The response says a stronger, larger base model can help GPT-5 develop better reasoning strategies and identifies a larger base model as one possible source of improvement.
